newsitem.title: USA: Business lunch drinking drastically reduced.
newsitem.headline: Business lunch drinking drastically reduced.

text.p: It's Tuesday lunch hour at the Brazilian Pavilion, where business executives dining under oil paintings of Latin landscapes prefer their cuisine with a Rio flavor.
On the white tablecloths, though, every one of the wine glasses stand stem up, untouched, as diners sip ice tea and soft drinks from water tumblers.

"Down, down, down, down, down!" is the way general manager Tony Duarte described the trend in lunchtime alcohol consumption since he opened his doors five years ago. "Only about 5 percent of our customers drink and they mostly drink beer and wine," he lamented.
"Do I drink at lunch?" one business executive reponded, pointing to his Coke. "I have to go back to work."
Owners of other restaurants also report business lunch drinking is way off.
At Ozio Martini and Cigar Lounge, Washington, D.C., general manager Dino Carr said, "We're drinking very little at lunch, maybe one martini -- not like at night."

"Ten or 15 years ago lunchtime drinking was much heavier," said Michael Sternberg, co-owner of Sam & Harry's, a Washington, D.C., steak house. "In a fine dining restaurant like ours, part of having a nice lunch is having a glass of wine. We also do a few scotches, a few martinis, here and there."

Rob Hoover, president of Sprint Staffing & Workforce USA, Tampa, attributed the decline to "the desire to be alert at work and an awareness among corporate executives of the impact drinking has on your health."
"Drinking is rare at the lunches I attend," Hoover said. "It's more likely to be Perrier than Johnny Walker."

"It's extremely unusual for people to drink now at lunch," agreed Barbara Crystal, a spokesperson for American Automobile Assn., Orlando. "The beverage of choice is probably iced tea. When I worked in New York (years ago) you'd have several drinks at lunch. I can't vouch for how much work I did in the afternoon."
Jeff Becker, vice president of alcohol issues at the Washington-based Beer Institute said there was definitely less drinking at lunctime.
"People are drinking less spirits at lunch and I think we and the wine people have definitely benefited from that. I have a beer at lunch probably only half the time," Becker said.
Besides concerns about after-lunch performance, tax changes have also played a role.

"Nobody wants a drunken executive in the afternoon," explained Dr. Cleaves Bennett, of Health Care Partners, Los Angeles, and author of "Control Your High Blood Pressure Without Drugs" (Doubleday). "And the tax code has discouraged expensive lunches for all concerned."

In 1994, noted Raymond Russolillo, of accountants Coopers & Lybrand, New York, the 80 percent deduction for a business lunch was cut to 50 percent. "I'm not so sure reduced drinking has to do so much with deductibility of expenses, which they (executives) pass on to their employers."
"I think people are working harder than ever and they're more concerned about their jobs and their clients and alcohol just gets in the way," Russolillo said."

"Twenty years ago it was pretty common to go with a customer to lunch and have a pop or two," recalled Rick Mohr, of Steelcase, the Grand Rapids, Mich., office furniture maker. "The social habits over lunch have changed with the awareness that they're supposed to be working sessions."

Noontime drinking is also taking a blow from employees who telescope their lunch hour. A recent Steelcase study found that, on average, office workers take 36 minutes for lunch each day, with 14 percent not taking any time at all, notably those in the $50,000-plus income bracket.
"The two-hour lunch is a thing of the past," Mohr said, as the lunch hour becomes "a catch-all for taking care of personal business as well as work-related activities."
One person who believes "people are seeing a return to a drink or two" at lunch is Elizabeth Board, director of public issues at the Washington-bsaed Distilled Spirits Council of the U.S.

"There was a time when people were very concerned--'Oh, I never eat red meat' -- each trying to outsalad the other person. But there's been a backlash that everything's unhealthy. I wouldn't say we're at the three martini lunch but there's certainly responsible drinking in moderation."
(Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace topics for Reuters. Any opinions expressed in this column are solely his own).
